title: Kenya
flagPageTitle: Flag of Kenya — Colors, Meaning & History
flagMetaDescription: Flag of Kenya: black, red and green bands with white fimbriations and a Maasai shield with crossed spears. Learn its colors, meaning and adoption date (1963).
flagMetaKeywords: kenya flag, flag of kenya, kenya flag colors, kenya flag meaning, maasai shield flag, kenyan flag history
flagSubtitle: Black, red and green bands with white fimbriations and a Maasai shield over crossed spears — the national flag of Kenya since independence.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of Kenya has three horizontal bands of black, red and green, separated by thin white fimbriations, with a Maasai shield and two crossed spears centered on the flag.
flagDescription: The Kenyan flag is a horizontal tricolor of black, red and green, separated by thin white stripes. At its center sits a traditional Maasai shield in black, red and white, crossed by two white spears. The proportion is 2:3 and the design has remained unchanged since independence in 1963.
flagColors: BlackRedGreenWhite
colorMeaningSummary: Black represents the people of Kenya, red stands for the blood shed during the struggle for independence, green symbolizes the country's natural wealth, and white represents peace and unity. The Maasai shield and spears represent the defense of freedom.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Black

Represents the indigenous African people of Kenya and the unity of the nation.

Red

Stands for the blood shed during the Mau Mau uprising and the broader struggle for independence.

Green

Symbolizes Kenya's fertile land, agriculture and natural wealth.

White

Represents peace and honesty, and the fimbriations separate the bands to avoid heraldic color contact.

Maasai shield

The traditional shield and crossed spears in the center represent the defense of the nation and its freedom.
flagHistory: The Kenyan flag was adopted on 12 December 1963, the day Kenya gained independence from the United Kingdom. It is based on the flag of the Kenya African National Union (KANU), the political party that led the independence movement, which used black, red and green with a shield and spears. A year later, when Kenya became a republic in 1964, the flag was retained and the white fimbriations were added to separate the black, red and green bands heraldically.
flagDesigner: Based on the KANU party flag
similarFlagsAnswer: The Kenyan flag shares its black-red-green color palette with Malawi and South Sudan, but only Kenya features a Maasai shield and crossed spears in the center.

title: Japan
flagPageTitle: Flag of Japan — Colors, Meaning & History
flagMetaDescription: Flag of Japan: a crimson disc on a white field. Learn its colors, meaning, adoption date (1999) and the history of the Hinomaru.
flagMetaKeywords: japan flag, flag of japan, japan flag colors, japan flag meaning, hinomaru, rising sun flag
flagSubtitle: A crimson disc centered on a white field — the Hinomaru, symbol of the rising sun.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of Japan is a white rectangle with a large crimson circle in the center, representing the sun. It is known as the Hinomaru, meaning 'circle of the sun'.
flagDescription: The Japanese flag is a white field with a crimson disc at its center, representing the sun. The diameter of the disc is three-fifths of the flag's height, and the flag proportion is 2:3. The design has been used unofficially since the 19th century and was formalized as the national flag by the Act on National Flag and Anthem in 1999.
flagColors: WhiteCrimson
colorMeaningSummary: White represents purity and honesty, and the crimson disc represents the sun, reflecting Japan's name — 'Land of the Rising Sun'. The design has deep cultural roots and was historically used on banners by samurai and during the Meiji period.
colorMeaningDetailed:
White

Represents purity, honesty and integrity — a value central to Japanese aesthetics and Shinto tradition.

Crimson

Represents sincerity, warmth and the sun itself. The specific shade used today is a bright, slightly pinkish red specified by the 1999 law.

Hinomaru (sun disc)

The red circle represents the rising sun, an ancient symbol of Japan and its imperial lineage. The name 'Japan' in Chinese characters (日本) literally means 'origin of the sun'.

Proportions

The 1999 law set the disc diameter to three-fifths of the flag's height, larger than many pre-modern versions of the Hinomaru.
flagHistory: The Hinomaru has been used in Japan since at least the 7th century, when it appeared on banners and court decorations. During the Edo period it was used on merchant ships, and in 1870 the Meiji government designated it for use on Japanese vessels. It served as the de facto national flag throughout the imperial era, but was only formally codified as the national flag on 13 August 1999 with the Act on National Flag and Anthem. The 1999 law also fixed the disc's proportions and the exact shade of red.
flagDesigner: Unknown — traditional design formalized by the Meiji government
similarFlagsAnswer: Bangladesh also uses a red disc, but on a green field and offset toward the hoist. Palau uses a yellow disc on a light blue field. Japan's white-and-red design is otherwise unique.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

The Rising Sun flag (Kyokujitsu-ki) — a sun with rays — is a distinct symbol used by the Japanese military since 1870 and remains in use by the Japan Self-Defense Forces. It is not the national flag and is not interchangeable with the Hinomaru.

  • Rising Sun Flag (1870–1945): Used by the Imperial Japanese Army and Navy, with 16 rays.
  • Japan Self-Defense Forces flag (1954–present): A modern version with adjusted proportions.
  • Meiji-era merchant flag: A smaller-disc Hinomaru used on civilian vessels before 1999.

title: Brazil
flagPageTitle: Flag of Brazil — Colors, Meaning & History
flagMetaDescription: Flag of Brazil: green field, yellow rhombus, blue celestial globe with 27 stars and the motto 'Ordem e Progresso'. Colors, meaning and 1889 adoption.
flagMetaKeywords: brazil flag, flag of brazil, brazil flag colors, brazil flag meaning, ordem e progresso, brazilian flag stars
flagSubtitle: A green field with a yellow rhombus, a blue celestial globe of 27 stars and the motto 'Ordem e Progresso'.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of Brazil has a green background, a yellow rhombus in the center, and a blue circle with 27 white stars and a white band reading 'Ordem e Progresso' ('Order and Progress').
flagDescription: The Brazilian flag consists of a green rectangle, a yellow rhombus centered on it, and a blue circle with white stars and a white equatorial band bearing the national motto 'Ordem e Progresso'. The flag proportion is 7:10. It was adopted on 19 November 1889, four days after the proclamation of the republic, and its current form (with 27 stars) dates from 1992.
flagColors: GreenYellowBlueWhite
colorMeaningSummary: Green represents the House of Braganza and Brazil's forests, yellow represents the House of Habsburg and the country's gold, and blue represents the sky over Rio de Janeiro on the morning of 15 November 1889. The 27 stars represent the 26 states and the Federal District, and the motto 'Ordem e Progresso' is inspired by Auguste Comte's positivism.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Green

Represents the forests of Brazil and the House of Braganza, the imperial dynasty that ruled Brazil until 1889.

Yellow

Represents Brazil's gold reserves and the House of Habsburg, to which Empress Maria Leopoldina belonged.

Blue

Represents the sky over Rio de Janeiro on 15 November 1889, the day the republic was proclaimed. The stars are arranged as seen from that location at that moment.

White

Used for the stars, the motto band and the border of the rhombus — representing peace and purity.

Stars

There are 27 stars — one for each state plus the Federal District. Nine star sizes correspond to the states' sizes on the actual Brazilian sky.

Ordem e Progresso

The motto means 'Order and Progress' and is derived from Auguste Comte's positivist slogan 'L'amour pour principe et l'ordre pour base; le progrès pour but'.
flagHistory: The Brazilian flag was adopted on 19 November 1889 by decree of the provisional republican government, four days after the monarchy was overthrown. It was designed by Raimundo Teixeira Mendes, Miguel Lemos, Manuel Pereira Reis and Décio Villares, drawing on the flag of the earlier Empire of Brazil (green field, yellow rhombus, imperial coat of arms). The republican design replaced the coat of arms with a blue celestial globe. The flag has been updated several times as new states were created — the most recent change added a 27th star in 1992.
flagDesigner: Raimundo Teixeira Mendes, Miguel Lemos, Manuel Pereira Reis, Décio Villares
similarFlagsAnswer: The Brazilian flag is unique among national flags for its astronomical globe. No other country's flag is closely comparable.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

Brazil has had several national flags since independence in 1822. Each was built around the same green-and-yellow palette but with different central emblems.

  • Empire of Brazil (1822–1889): Green field, yellow rhombus, imperial coat of arms in the center.
  • Republic (1889–1960): The current design with 21 stars, adding one per new state over time.
  • Republic (1960–1992): 22 stars after the creation of Guanabara and later the Federal District.
  • Current version (1992–present): 27 stars, matching the current federal units.

title: South Africa
flagPageTitle: Flag of South Africa — Colors, Meaning & History
flagMetaDescription: Flag of South Africa: a Y-shaped design in black, green, yellow, white, red and blue. Learn its colors, meaning and 1994 adoption date.
flagMetaKeywords: south africa flag, flag of south africa, south africa flag colors, south africa flag meaning, y flag, six color flag
flagCaption: Flag of South Africa, adopted 27 April 1994
flagSubtitle: Six colors in a Y-shaped design — one of the most colorful national flags in the world.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of South Africa has a horizontal Y-shaped design combining black, green, yellow, white, red and blue, with a black triangle at the hoist edged in yellow.
flagDescription: The South African flag is composed of a horizontal Y-shape (a heraldic pall) with a black isosceles triangle at the hoist, edged in yellow. The upper arm is red and the lower arm is blue, both bordered in white, with green forming the center of the Y. The design uses six colors — black, green, yellow, white, red and blue — making it one of the most colorful national flags in the world.
flagColors: BlackYellowGreenWhiteRedBlue
colorMeaningSummary: The design deliberately combines colors from both the previous national flag (orange, white and blue) and the African National Congress flag (black, green and yellow), symbolizing unity after apartheid. Black represents the people, green represents the land, yellow represents mineral wealth, white represents peace, red represents the blood shed for freedom, and blue represents the sky and oceans.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Black

Represents the Black African majority and, more broadly, the people of South Africa.

Green

Represents the land and its natural environment.

Yellow

Represents the country's mineral wealth, particularly gold.

White

Represents peace and the European population, included to signal reconciliation.

Red

Represents the blood shed during the struggle for freedom and independence.

Blue

Represents the sky and the two oceans that surround the country — the Atlantic and the Indian.

Y-shape

Represents the convergence of diverse peoples and traditions into one nation, and the road ahead.
flagHistory: The South African flag was designed by Frederick Brownell, then State Herald of South Africa, and adopted on 27 April 1994 — the day of the first democratic elections following the end of apartheid. It was intended to be an interim flag used for five years, but was retained because of its widespread popularity. The design combines colors from both the pre-1994 flag (orange, white, blue) and the ANC flag (black, green, yellow), deliberately avoiding any direct reference to either side of the apartheid conflict.
flagDesigner: Frederick Brownell
similarFlagsAnswer: No other national flag closely resembles South Africa's. The six-color composition and Y-shape are unique in vexillology.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

Before 1994, South Africa used several different flags, each reflecting a different political era.

  • Union of South Africa (1928–1994): Orange, white and blue horizontal bands with miniature Union Jack, Orange Free State and Transvaal flags in the center.
  • Apartheid-era flag (1961–1994): Same as the Union flag after South Africa became a republic.
  • 1910–1928: A red ensign variant used after the Union of South Africa was formed.
  • Interim flag (1994–present): The current six-color design, originally intended as a five-year interim flag.

title: Germany
flagPageTitle: Flag of Germany — Colors, Meaning & History
flagMetaDescription: Flag of Germany: three horizontal bands of black, red and gold. Learn its colors, meaning, adoption date (1949) and the history of Schwarz-Rot-Gold.
flagMetaKeywords: germany flag, flag of germany, germany flag colors, germany flag meaning, schwarz rot gold, german tricolor
flagSubtitle: Three horizontal bands of black, red and gold — the Schwarz-Rot-Gold of the 1848 revolution.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of Germany is a horizontal tricolor of black, red and gold (golden yellow) in three equal bands.
flagDescription: The German flag consists of three equal horizontal bands of black, red and gold. The flag proportion is 3:5. It was adopted in its current form on 23 May 1949 for West Germany and retained after reunification in 1990. The colors trace back to the uniforms of the Lützow Free Corps during the Napoleonic Wars and became the symbol of the 1848 German revolution.
flagColors: BlackRedGold
colorMeaningSummary: The colors originated with the Lützow Free Corps during the Napoleonic Wars and became the symbol of the 1848 German revolution and the struggle for a unified, democratic Germany. Black represents determination and dignity, red represents bravery and hardiness, and gold represents generosity and the aspiration for freedom and unity.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Black

Represents determination, dignity and, historically, the dark uniforms of the Lützow Free Corps.

Red

Represents bravery, hardiness and the blood shed in the struggle for German unity.

Gold

Represents generosity, freedom and the golden buttons on the Free Corps' uniforms. Officially a golden yellow, not a metallic gold.

Origin (1813)

The Lützow Free Corps — a volunteer unit during the Napoleonic Wars — wore black uniforms with red trim and gold buttons. Members popularized the color combination on their return to civilian life.

1848 revolution

The Frankfurt Parliament adopted black-red-gold as the flag of a unified German state, cementing its association with liberal and democratic ideals.
flagHistory: The black-red-gold tricolor was first adopted by the Frankfurt Parliament in 1848 as the flag of a unified, democratic Germany. The Weimar Republic (1919–1933) used it as the national flag. The Nazi regime replaced it with a red flag bearing a swastika from 1933 to 1945. After World War II, both West Germany (1949) and East Germany (1949) adopted the black-red-gold tricolor. East Germany added a hammer-and-compass emblem in 1959, which West Germany considered a violation of the shared flag. On 3 October 1990, reunification restored the plain tricolor as the flag of a single Germany.
flagDesigner: Unknown — derived from the Lützow Free Corps uniforms
similarFlagsAnswer: Belgium uses vertical black-yellow-red bands, and the Netherlands uses horizontal red-white-blue. Germany is the only country with horizontal black-red-gold.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

Germany has had several national flags across different political eras. The black-red-gold tricolor is not the only design the country has used.

  • German Empire (1871–1918): Black-white-red horizontal tricolor.
  • Weimar Republic (1919–1933): Black-red-gold tricolor.
  • Nazi Germany (1933–1945): Red flag with a black swastika on a white disc.
  • East Germany (1949–1990): Black-red-gold with a hammer, compass and ring of rye.
  • West Germany (1949–1990): Plain black-red-gold tricolor.
  • Reunified Germany (1990–present): Plain black-red-gold tricolor.

title: France
flagPageTitle: Flag of France — Colors, Meaning & History
flagMetaDescription: Flag of France: three vertical bands of blue, white and red. Learn its colors, meaning, adoption date (1794) and the history of the Tricolore.
flagMetaKeywords: france flag, flag of france, french flag, france flag colors, france flag meaning, tricolore, bleu blanc rouge
flagSubtitle: Three vertical bands of blue, white and red — the Tricolore, symbol of the French Revolution.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of France is a vertical tricolor of blue, white and red in three equal bands. It is known as the Tricolore.
flagDescription: The French flag consists of three equal vertical bands of blue (hoist), white (center) and red (fly). The proportion is 2:3. It was adopted on 15 February 1794 during the French Revolution and has remained the national flag ever since, with only brief interruptions in 1814–1830 and 1848.
flagColors: BlueWhiteRed
colorMeaningSummary: Blue and red are the traditional colors of Paris, worn by the militia that stormed the Bastille in 1789. White was the color of the Bourbon monarchy. Combined, they represent the union of the people and the crown under the new republic — and are popularly said to stand for liberty, equality and fraternity.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Blue

The traditional color of Paris, associated with Saint Martin and the city's militia. Often linked to liberty.

White

The color of the Bourbon monarchy and the royal standard of France before the Revolution. Placed between blue and red, it represents peace and the reconciliation of the nation.

Red

The traditional color of Paris, associated with Saint Denis and the revolutionary flag of 1789. Often linked to equality and the blood of the revolution.

Liberty, Equality, Fraternity

The popular association of blue, white and red with the national motto is a 19th-century interpretation, not part of the original design.
flagHistory: The Tricolore emerged during the French Revolution. On 13 July 1789, the day before the storming of the Bastille, Parisian militia adopted a cockade of blue and red — the city's colors. On 17 July, Lafayette added white to create a national cockade combining the colors of Paris with the royal white. A flag based on this cockade was adopted by the National Convention on 15 February 1794. It was briefly replaced during the Bourbon Restoration (1814–1830) and the Second Republic (1848), but has been the national flag continuously since 1830.
flagDesigner: Lafayette (cockade origin)
similarFlagsAnswer: The Netherlands and Luxembourg also use vertical blue-white-red tricolors, but with different proportions and shades. France's blue is darker and Luxembourg's blue is lighter.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

France has changed its national flag several times, and the Tricolore itself has been used in several configurations.

  • Kingdom of France (pre-1789): White flag with golden fleurs-de-lis.
  • Bourbon Restoration (1814–1830): Plain white flag.
  • July Monarchy (1830–1848): Tricolore with a restored cockade.
  • Second Republic (1848): Briefly red flag considered, then Tricolore retained.
  • Vichy France (1940–1944): Tricolore with a Francisque emblem.
  • Free France (1940–1944): Tricolore with a red Cross of Lorraine.

title: Italy

flagMetaDescription: Flag of Italy: three vertical bands of green, white and red. Learn its colors, meaning, adoption date (1946) and the history of the Tricolore Italiano.
flagMetaKeywords: italy flag, flag of italy, italian flag, italy flag colors, italy flag meaning, tricolore italiano
flagSubtitle: Three vertical bands of green, white and red — the Tricolore Italiano, born in the Napoleonic era.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of Italy is a vertical tricolor of green, white and red in three equal bands.
flagDescription: The Italian flag consists of three equal vertical bands of green (hoist), white (center) and red (fly). The proportion is 2:3. It was adopted on 1 January 1948 with the constitution of the Italian Republic, though the design dates back to 1797 when it was first used by the Cispadane Republic.
flagColors: GreenWhiteRed
colorMeaningSummary: Green represents the Italian landscape and hope, white represents the snow of the Alps and peace, and red represents the blood shed for Italian independence. The colors originate from the uniforms of the Milanese Civic Guard and the French Tricolore, adapted during the Napoleonic era.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Green

Represents the Italian countryside, hope and the Lombard Legion's green uniforms.

White

Represents the snow of the Alps, peace and, in some interpretations, the Catholic faith.

Red

Represents the blood shed in the wars of Italian independence and unification.

Origin (1796)

The colors first appeared on the tricolor of the Lombard Legion, then on the flag of the Cispadane Republic in 1797 — modeled after the French Tricolore but with green replacing blue.
flagHistory: The Italian tricolor was first adopted by the Cispadane Republic on 7 January 1797, in Reggio Emilia, based on the French Tricolore with green replacing blue. It was used by various Italian states during the Napoleonic era and became a symbol of the Risorgimento — the movement for Italian unification. The Kingdom of Italy adopted it in 1861 with the royal Savoy coat of arms in the center. When Italy became a republic in 1946, the coat of arms was removed, and the plain tricolor was formally adopted on 1 January 1948.
flagDesigner: Giuseppe Compagnoni (Cispadane Republic)
similarFlagsAnswer: Mexico uses a vertical green-white-red tricolor with a coat of arms in the center. Ireland uses green-white-orange. Italy's plain green-white-red is unique among national flags.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

Italy has used several versions of the tricolor before the current plain design was adopted.

  • Cispadane Republic (1797): First green-white-red tricolor.
  • Kingdom of Italy (1861–1946): Tricolor with the Savoy coat of arms in the center.
  • Italian Social Republic (1943–1945): Tricolor with a fasces emblem.
  • Italian Republic (1948–present): Plain green-white-red tricolor.

title: Spain
flagPageTitle: Flag of Spain — Colors, Meaning & History
flagMetaDescription: Flag of Spain: red, yellow and red horizontal bands with the coat of arms. Learn its colors, meaning, adoption date (1981) and the history of the Rojigualda.
flagMetaKeywords: spain flag, flag of spain, spanish flag, spain flag colors, spain flag meaning, rojigualda, bandera de españa
flagSubtitle: Red, yellow and red horizontal bands with the Spanish coat of arms — the Rojigualda.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of Spain has three horizontal bands of red, yellow and red, with the yellow band twice as wide as each red band. The Spanish coat of arms sits on the hoist side of the yellow band.
flagDescription: The Spanish flag is a horizontal tricolor of red, yellow and red, with the yellow band twice the height of each red band. The coat of arms of Spain appears on the hoist side of the yellow band. The proportion is 2:3. The current design was formalized by the Spanish Constitution of 1978 and the Flag Law of 1981.
flagColors: RedYellow
colorMeaningSummary: Red represents the blood shed by Spaniards in defense of the nation, and yellow represents the wealth and generosity of the country. The colors are traditional heraldic colors of the Spanish kingdoms and have been used together since the 18th century.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Red

Represents bravery, strength and the blood shed by Spaniards in defense of the nation. Red is also a traditional color of the Crown of Castile.

Yellow

Represents generosity, wealth and the gold of the Spanish Empire. It is a traditional heraldic color of the Crown of Aragon.

Coat of arms

Displays the quartered arms of Castile, León, Aragon and Navarre, with Granada at the base, the Pillars of Hercules on either side and the Bourbon-Anjou escutcheon in the center.
flagHistory: The red-yellow-red design was chosen by King Charles III in 1785 to distinguish Spanish naval ships from those of other nations, which used similar white ensigns. It was known as the Rojigualda. The design became the national flag in 1843 under Queen Isabella II. The current coat of arms was added in 1981, replacing the earlier version used under Franco, and reflects the constitutional monarchy established in 1978.
flagDesigner: Antonio Valdés y Fernández Bazán (naval origin)
similarFlagsAnswer: No other national flag uses the same red-yellow-red arrangement with an off-center coat of arms. Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela use yellow-blue-red horizontal bands, which are related by history but visually distinct.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

Spain has used several national flags across its history, and different political eras used different coats of arms on the same Rojigualda base.

  • Bourbon Spain (1785–1873): Rojigualda with the Bourbon coat of arms.
  • First Spanish Republic (1873–1874): Rojigualda with a crowned or uncrowned republican variant.
  • Second Spanish Republic (1931–1939): Rojigualda with a mural crown and purple stripe replacing the lower red band.
  • Francoist Spain (1939–1977): Rojigualda with the Eagle of Saint John.
  • Current flag (1981–present): Rojigualda with the constitutional coat of arms.

countryNameLocal: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
flagCaption: Flag of the United Kingdom, adopted 1 January 1801
flagSubtitle: The Union Jack — the crosses of St George, St Andrew and St Patrick combined into one flag.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of the United Kingdom is the Union Jack: a blue field with the red cross of St George edged in white, overlain with the white diagonal cross of St Andrew and the red diagonal cross of St Patrick.
flagDescription: The Union Jack combines three heraldic crosses: the red cross of St George (England) on a white ground, the white saltire of St Andrew (Scotland) on a blue field, and the red saltire of St Patrick (Ireland). The proportion is 1:2 for land use and 1:2 at sea. The flag was adopted on 1 January 1801 with the Act of Union that joined the Kingdom of Great Britain and the Kingdom of Ireland.
flagColors: BlueWhiteRed
colorMeaningSummary: Blue represents the sea and St Andrew's saltire, white represents peace and St Andrew's cross, and red represents the crosses of St George and St Patrick. The three crosses together represent the union of England, Scotland and Ireland under one crown.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Blue

The field of the flag and the background of the Scottish saltire. Represents the sea, truth and loyalty.

White

The border of St George's cross and the saltire of St Andrew. Represents peace and purity.

Red

The cross of St George (England) and the saltire of St Patrick (Ireland). Represents strength, bravery and the blood of the union's defenders.

St George's Cross

A red cross on white, the national flag of England since the Middle Ages.

St Andrew's Saltire

A white diagonal cross on blue, the national flag of Scotland.

St Patrick's Saltire

A red diagonal cross on white, representing Ireland in the union.
flagHistory: The first Union Flag was created in 1606, combining the crosses of St George (England) and St Andrew (Scotland) after the Union of the Crowns in 1603. The current design dates from 1 January 1801, when the Act of Union joined Great Britain and Ireland and the cross of St Patrick was added. The flag has remained unchanged since, even after the partition of Ireland in 1921, because the cross of St Patrick continues to represent Northern Ireland in the union.
flagDesigner: Unknown — heraldic design formalized by royal proclamation
similarFlagsAnswer: No other national flag closely resembles the Union Jack. Hawaii incorporates it in its canton as a historical reference to British influence.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

The Union Jack has had several forms across the history of the British Isles.

  • First Union Flag (1606–1801): Crosses of St George and St Andrew only, without St Patrick's saltire.
  • Current Union Jack (1801–present): Adds the cross of St Patrick for Ireland.
  • Commonwealth flags: Australia, New Zealand, Tuvalu and Fiji incorporate the Union Jack in their cantons.
  • Hawaii state flag: Uses the Union Jack in the canton, a legacy of British influence in the 19th century.

title: United States

flagMetaDescription: Flag of the United States: 13 stripes and 50 stars on a blue canton. Learn its colors, meaning, adoption date (1777) and the history of the Stars and Stripes.

flagCaption: Flag of the United States, adopted 14 June 1777 (current 50-star version 4 July 1960)
flagSubtitle: Thirteen stripes and fifty stars — the Stars and Stripes, symbol of the American republic.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of the United States has 13 horizontal stripes of red and white, and a blue canton with 50 white stars. The stripes represent the original 13 colonies, and the stars represent the 50 states.
flagDescription: The United States flag consists of 13 equal horizontal stripes of red and white, alternating with red at the top and bottom, and a blue rectangle in the canton bearing 50 white five-pointed stars arranged in nine offset rows. The proportion is 10:19. The flag has been modified 26 times since 1777, most recently on 4 July 1960 with the admission of Hawaii.
flagColors: RedWhiteBlue
colorMeaningSummary: Red represents hardiness and valor, white represents purity and innocence, and blue represents vigilance, perseverance and justice. The 13 stripes represent the original 13 colonies that declared independence from Britain, and the 50 stars represent the current 50 states.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Red

Represents hardiness and valor, and the blood shed in the fight for independence.

White

Represents purity and innocence.

Blue

Represents vigilance, perseverance and justice, and is the color of the canton field.

Thirteen stripes

Represent the 13 British colonies that declared independence in 1776: Delaware, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Georgia, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Maryland, South Carolina, New Hampshire, Virginia, New York, North Carolina and Rhode Island.

Fifty stars

One star for each state. A new star is added on the 4th of July following the admission of a new state.
flagHistory: The first American flag was adopted by the Continental Congress on 14 June 1777, though the exact origin of the design is uncertain. The popular legend credits Betsy Ross, but no contemporary evidence confirms her role. The flag has been modified 26 times since — once for each new state admitted to the union. Legend of the parihuanas

According to tradition, General José de San Martín landed at Paracas in 1820 and saw flocks of parihuanas — Andean flamingos with red and white plumage — rising into the air. He chose those colors for the new flag of independent Peru.

Coat of arms

The state flag includes the Peruvian coat of arms, which features a vicuña (national animal), a cinchona tree (source of quinine) and a cornucopia spilling golden coins, representing Peru's natural wealth.
flagHistory: Peru declared independence from Spain on 28 July 1821, and General José de San Martín designed the first Peruvian flag — a version with four diagonal sections in red and white. In 1825, Simón Bolívar standardized the flag as a vertical red-white-red tricolor, which remains in use today. The black and white stripes are also inspired by the zebra, the national animal of Botswana. Zebras are common in Botswana's national parks, particularly the Okavango Delta and Chobe National Park.

Represents patriotism, valor, courage and the blood shed by Filipino patriots in the struggle for independence — first against Spain and later against the United States and Japan.

White triangle

Represents equality, fraternity and purity — ideals drawn from the French Revolution and the Katipunan movement, which sought independence from Spanish colonial rule.

Golden sun

Represents liberty and independence. The eight rays of the sun represent the eight provinces that were placed under martial law by the Spanish colonial government during the Philippine Revolution of 1896: Manila, Cavite, Bulacan, Pampanga, Nueva Ecija, Tarlac, Laguna and Batangas.

Three stars

Represent the three main island groups of the Philippines — Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao — and the unity of the Filipino people.

War flag

When the Philippines is at war, the flag is flown with red on top and blue on the bottom — reversing the peacetime arrangement. This makes the Philippine flag unique among national flags for its wartime reversal.
flagHistory: The Philippine flag was designed by General Emilio Aguinaldo, the first president of the Philippines, and was first raised on 12 June 1898, when the Philippines declared independence from Spain. The design was based on the flag of the Katipunan, the revolutionary society that had fought against Spanish rule since 1896. During the Philippine–American War (1899–1902), the flag was banned by the American colonial government. It was reauthorized in 1919 and became the national flag when the Philippines became a Commonwealth in 1935. During the Japanese occupation (1942–1945), the flag was used by the Philippine Commonwealth government-in-exile. The current proportions and design were standardized in 1998 with the passage of Republic Act No. 8491. The flag has remained unchanged since.
flagDesigner: Emilio Aguinaldo (design), Marcela Agoncillo (sewing)

flagHistory: Korea was under Japanese colonial rule from 1910 until 1945, when it was liberated at the end of World War II. Blue

Represents the 'Munkh Khukh Tenger' — the eternal blue sky — which is the central spiritual concept of Mongolian traditional belief. Blue also represents the vast open steppes that define Mongolia's landscape.

Soyombo symbol

The golden Soyombo symbol is the national emblem of Mongolia and appears on the flag's hoist side. It consists of several elements, each with its own meaning: the flame at the top represents eternal growth and the revival of the nation; the sun and moon represent the eternal existence of the Mongol nation; the arrows represent the defense of the nation; the rectangles represent honesty and justice; the yin-yang symbol at the base represents the balance of male and female principles.
flagHistory: Mongolia declared independence from China in 1911, following the collapse of the Qing dynasty, and became a Soviet-aligned socialist state in 1924 as the Mongolian People's Republic. The first Mongolian flag was a red flag with the Soyombo symbol in the center and the Mongolian script on the side. In 1940, the flag was changed to a red field with the Soyombo symbol in the center, and later variations included a blue band added to the design. After the democratic revolution of 1990, the communist star was removed from the flag, and on 12 February 1992, the current design was adopted — red, blue and red vertical bands with the Soyombo symbol in the left red band. flagHistory: The modern Chinese flag was created during the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949. The flag was approved by the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference in September 1949 and was first raised in Beijing on 1 October 1949, when the People's Republic of China was proclaimed. Red field

Three colors

The Republic of China formally adopted the current design as its national flag in 1928 under the Nationalist government. After the Chinese Civil War, the government of the Republic of China relocated to Taiwan in 1949, while the People's Republic of China was established on the mainland. White shahada

The shahada is the Islamic declaration of faith — 'There is no god but God; Muhammad is the messenger of God'. It is the first of the Five Pillars of Islam and represents the central belief of the Saudi state and people.

White sword

Double-sided design

flagHistory: The first Saudi state was established in 1744 in Diriyah and used a green banner with the shahada. The sword was originally curved; in 1973, it was changed to a straight horizontal sword, and the shahada was enlarged and redesigned with modern calligraphy. Both states used versions of the Arab Liberation Flag — red, white and black horizontal bands — with different emblems in the center. On 22 May 1990, the two Yemens unified to form the Republic of Yemen, and the unified flag was adopted — the plain red, white and black tricolor without any emblem, symbolizing the unity of the two former states. flagSubtitle: Red, white and black bands with the Takbir in green — the flag of the Republic of Iraq.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of Iraq has three equal horizontal bands of red (top), white (middle) and black (bottom), with the Takbir — 'God is great' — written in green Kufic script in the center of the white band. The proportion is 2:3.
flagDescription: The Iraqi flag consists of three equal horizontal bands of red (top), white (middle) and black (bottom), with the Arabic phrase 'الله أكبر' (Allahu Akbar, 'God is great') written in green Kufic script in the center of the white band. The proportion is 2:3. The current design was adopted on 22 January 2008, when the three stars that had previously appeared alongside the Takbir were removed.
flagColors: RedWhiteBlackGreen
colorMeaningSummary: Red represents courage, the blood shed for Iraqi independence and the sacrifice of Iraqi martyrs, white represents peace and a bright future, and black represents the dark years of oppression under foreign rule and the country's oil wealth. The green Takbir represents Islam and the unity of the Iraqi people.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Red

Represents courage, the blood shed by Iraqi patriots in the struggle for independence from the Ottoman Empire and later from British rule, and the sacrifices of Iraqi martyrs in the country's many wars.

White

Represents peace, purity and hope for a bright future. White is the middle band and provides a neutral background for the green Takbir.

Black

Represents the dark years of oppression under Ottoman and British colonial rule, and the country's oil wealth — Iraq has some of the largest oil reserves in the world. Black is also a traditional color of the Abbasid Caliphate, which ruled from Baghdad for five centuries.

Green Takbir

The Takbir — 'God is great' — represents Islam and the unity of the Iraqi people. Green is the traditional color of Islam and is used to write the Takbir on the flag.

Arab Liberation colors

The red, white and black bands are the Arab Liberation colors, first used by the Free Officers movement in Egypt in 1952 and later adopted by several Arab states. Iraq's flag is one of four Arab flags (along with Egypt, Syria and Yemen) that use this color scheme.
flagHistory: Iraq was part of the Ottoman Empire until World War I, when it was captured by British forces and became a British mandate. The first Iraqi flag was adopted in 1921, when Faisal I was installed as king — it featured the Arab Revolt colors (black, white and green) with a red triangle and two white stars. In 1958, following a military coup that overthrew the monarchy, the flag was changed to a red, white and black design with a yellow sun and a red star in the center, inspired by the Arab Liberation Flag. In 1963, three green stars were added to the white band. In 1991, following the Gulf War, the Takbir was added between the stars in Saddam Hussein's own handwriting. In 2004, following the fall of Saddam Hussein, the script was changed to a more modern Kufic font, and in 2008, the three stars were removed, leaving the current design.
flagDesigner: Based on the 1963 Arab Liberation Flag design
similarFlagsAnswer: Egypt, Syria and Yemen use the same red-white-black tricolor with different emblems in the white band — Egypt with the Eagle of Saladin, Syria with two green stars, and Yemen with no emblem. Iraq uses the green Takbir as its emblem.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

Iraq has used several flags since its establishment in 1921.

  • Kingdom of Iraq (1921–1959): Black, white and green bands with a red triangle and two white stars.
  • Republic of Iraq (1959–1963): Red, white and black bands with a yellow sun and a red star.
  • Republic of Iraq (1963–1991): Red, white and black bands with three green stars.
  • Republic of Iraq (1991–2004): Same design with the Takbir added between the stars.
  • Republic of Iraq (2004–2008): Same design with the Takbir in modern Kufic script.
  • Current flag (2008–present): Takbir only, no stars.

flagDescription: The current Syrian flag consists of three horizontal bands of green (top), white (middle) and black (bottom), with three red five-pointed stars centered in the white band. The proportion is 2:3. This design was originally adopted in 1932 for the Syrian Republic under the French mandate, was used until 1958, and was restored in 2025 following the fall of the Ba'athist government. A different design — red, white and black bands with two green stars — was used from 1980 to 2025.
flagColors: GreenWhiteBlackRed
colorMeaningSummary: Green represents the Fatimid Caliphate and the fertility of the Syrian land, white represents the Umayyad Caliphate and peace, black represents the Abbasid Caliphate and the dark years of oppression, and the three red stars represent the three districts that made up the original Syrian Republic — Aleppo, Damascus and the Euphrates region — and the blood shed for Syrian independence.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Green band

Represents the Fatimid Caliphate and the fertility of the Syrian land, including its agricultural regions along the Orontes and Euphrates rivers.

White band

Represents the Umayyad Caliphate, whose capital was Damascus, and peace and purity. Damascus was the seat of the Umayyad Caliphate from 661 to 750 CE.

Black band

Represents the Abbasid Caliphate, which ruled from Baghdad, and the dark years of foreign rule. Black is also a Pan-Arab color.

Three red stars

Represent the three districts that made up the original Syrian Republic under the French mandate — the State of Aleppo, the State of Damascus and the Alawite State (later the Sanjak of Latakia). The stars also represent the blood shed for Syrian independence.

Historical context

The green-white-black design with three red stars was first adopted in 1932 and was the flag of Syria from independence in 1946 until the union with Egypt in 1958. It was restored in 2025 following the fall of the Ba'athist government in December 2024. The red-white-black design with two green stars used from 1980 to 2025 was associated with the Ba'ath Party and its rule.
flagHistory: Syria was part of the Ottoman Empire until 1918, then became a French mandate after World War I. The first Syrian flag, adopted in 1920 under the short-lived Arab Kingdom of Syria, was based on the Arab Revolt flag. Under the French mandate, a new design was adopted in 1932 — green, white and black bands with three red stars representing the three districts of the mandate. This flag was retained when Syria gained independence in 1946. In 1958, Syria united with Egypt to form the United Arab Republic, and the flag was changed to a red, white and black tricolor with two green stars. After the UAR dissolved in 1961, Syria briefly restored the 1932 flag, then changed to a red-white-black design with three green stars, and later (in 1980) to a red-white-black design with two green stars. In December 2024, the Ba'athist government fell, and in 2025 the independence flag was restored as the national flag.
flagDesigner: Based on the original 1932 Syrian Republic flag
similarFlagsAnswer: Iraq, Yemen and Egypt use red, white and black bands with different emblems. Syria's current design uses green, white and black bands — a different order — with three red stars, distinguishing it from the other Arab tricolors.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

Syria has used several flags across its mandate, independence, union and Ba'athist periods.

  • Arab Kingdom of Syria (1920): Arab Revolt flag with black, white and green bands and a red triangle.
  • French Mandate (1922–1932): Various French-inspired designs.
  • Syrian Republic (1932–1958): Green, white and black bands with three red stars.
  • United Arab Republic (1958–1961): Red, white and black with two green stars.
  • Syrian Arab Republic (1961–1963): Independence flag briefly restored.
  • Ba'athist Syria (1963–1980): Red, white and black with three green stars, then two.
  • Ba'athist Syria (1980–2024): Red, white and black with two green stars.
  • Current flag (2025–present): Independence flag restored with green, white and black bands and three red stars.

title: Lebanon

flagSubtitle: Red and white bands with a green cedar tree — the flag of the Lebanese Republic.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of Lebanon has three horizontal bands — red (top), white (center, twice as wide) and red (bottom) — with a green cedar tree centered on the white band. The proportion is 2:3.
flagDescription: The Lebanese flag consists of three horizontal bands — a red band at the top, a wider white band in the center, and a red band at the bottom — with a green cedar tree centered on the white band. The proportion is 2:3. The flag was adopted on 7 December 1943, when Lebanon gained independence from France, and has remained unchanged since.
flagColors: RedWhiteGreen
colorMeaningSummary: Red represents the blood shed for Lebanese independence and the courage of the Lebanese people, white represents peace and the snow of the Lebanese mountains, and the green cedar tree represents the country's national symbol — the Cedar of Lebanon, mentioned in the Bible and used as a symbol of strength and eternity for millennia.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Red bands

Represent the blood shed by Lebanese patriots in the struggle for independence from the Ottoman Empire and later from French mandate rule, and the courage and determination of the Lebanese people.

White band

Represents peace and the snow that covers the peaks of the Lebanon Mountains, which run the length of the country. White is also a color of purity and hope.

Cedar tree

The green cedar tree in the center is the national symbol of Lebanon — the Cedar of Lebanon (Cedrus libani), which has grown on Mount Lebanon for thousands of years. The cedar has been a symbol of strength, eternity and resilience since ancient times, and it appears in the Bible, in Mesopotamian texts and on Phoenician coins. The tree on the flag is a stylized version of the Lebanese cedar, and it appears on the country's coat of arms, currency and postage stamps.

Symbolism of the cedar

The cedar has been used as a symbol of Lebanon since the 17th century, when Maronite Christians adopted it as an emblem. It was also used on the flag of the State of Greater Lebanon under the French mandate (1920–1943). Its placement on the flag emphasizes its central role in Lebanese national identity.
flagHistory: Lebanon was part of the Ottoman Empire from 1516 until 1918, when it was captured by Allied forces during World War I. From 1920 to 1943, Lebanon was a French mandate territory, and its flag during this period was the French tricolor with a green cedar tree in the center of the white band. On 7 December 1943, Lebanon gained independence from France, and the current flag was adopted. The design was created by Henri Pharaon, a Lebanese MP, who proposed using the colors of the French flag but with the cedar tree as the central emblem. The flag has remained unchanged since, including through the Lebanese Civil War (1975–1990) and the country's subsequent political crises. There have been several proposals to change the flag to add other Lebanese symbols, but none have been adopted.
flagDesigner: Henri Pharaon, with input from the Lebanese government
similarFlagsAnswer: Austria uses red-white-red horizontal bands without an emblem. Peru uses vertical red-white-red bands with a coat of arms on the state version. Lebanon's horizontal red-white-red bands with a central cedar tree is unique.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

Lebanon has used several flags across its Ottoman, mandate and independence periods.

  • First independence flag (1943): Current design adopted.

  • Presidential standard: Uses the Lebanese coat of arms with a cedar tree and two red bands.

title: Israel

flagDescription: The Israeli flag consists of a white field with two horizontal blue stripes — one near the top edge and one near the bottom edge — and a blue six-pointed Star of David centered between them. The proportion is 8:11. It was adopted on 28 October 1948, five months after the establishment of the State of Israel, and has remained unchanged since.
flagColors: WhiteBlue
colorMeaningSummary: White represents purity, honesty and peace, and blue represents the sky, faith and the traditional blue of Jewish prayer shawls. The Star of David is a symbol of Judaism and Jewish identity, and the two stripes evoke the tallit (Jewish prayer shawl), which has blue or black stripes near its ends.
colorMeaningDetailed:
White

Represents purity, honesty and peace. White is also the background color of the traditional Jewish prayer shawl, the tallit, which inspired the design.

Blue stripes

The two blue stripes represent the stripes on the tallit, the Jewish prayer shawl worn during prayer. The blue color is associated with tekhelet, a blue dye mentioned in the Torah and used in ancient Jewish ritual garments. Blue also represents the sky and the heavens, and the connection between the Jewish people and the land of Israel.

Star of David

The blue six-pointed star in the center is the Magen David ('Shield of David'), which has been a symbol of Judaism and Jewish identity since the Middle Ages. It became the central emblem of the Zionist movement in the late 19th century and was used on the flag of the World Zionist Organization, designed by David Wolffsohn in 1891. The star appears on the flag as two overlapping triangles, with no fill.

Design origin

The design was based on the flag of the World Zionist Organization, which was itself inspired by the tallit. The State of Israel adopted it as the national flag on 28 October 1948, five months after declaring independence on 14 May 1948.
flagHistory: The Zionist flag — a white field with blue stripes and a blue Star of David — was first designed by David Wolffsohn for the World Zionist Organization in 1891, inspired by the traditional Jewish prayer shawl. It was used by Zionist organizations and Jewish communities around the world for decades before the establishment of the State of Israel. On 14 May 1948, Israel declared independence, and on 28 October 1948, the flag was formally adopted by the Provisional Council of State. The design was chosen over several alternatives, including a proposal to include a menorah or the Tablets of the Law. The flag has remained unchanged since, including the exact shade of blue, which has been the subject of some debate (the current shade is a dark blue, sometimes called 'Israeli blue').
flagDesigner: David Wolffsohn (original Zionist design, 1891)
similarFlagsAnswer: No other national flag closely resembles Israel's. The combination of a white field with two blue stripes and a central Star of David is unique, though it is sometimes compared to the flag of Greece (blue and white with a cross).
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

Israel has used several flags across its Zionist movement and modern statehood periods.

  • World Zionist Organization (1891–1948): White field with blue stripes and a blue Star of David.
  • Jewish Brigade (1944–1946): Zionist flag used by Jewish volunteers in the British Army.
  • State of Israel (1948–present): Current design adopted by the Provisional Council of State.
  • Presidential standard: Uses the Israeli coat of arms with a menorah and olive branches.
  • Naval ensign: Uses a design similar to the national flag with a darker shade of blue and a different layout.

title: Afghanistan

flagCaption: Flag of Afghanistan — status contested since 2021
flagSubtitle: Black, red and green bands with the national emblem — the flag of the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, contested since 2021.
flagQuickAnswer: The internationally recognized flag of Afghanistan has three vertical bands of black (hoist), red (center) and green (fly), with the national emblem in white in the center of the red band. The proportion is 2:3. A different black-and-white flag has been used by the Taliban government since 2021.
flagDescription: Afghanistan's flag status has been contested since the Taliban took power in August 2021. The internationally recognized flag of the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan consists of three vertical bands of black (hoist), red (center) and green (fly), with the national emblem in white in the center of the red band. The Taliban government uses a different flag — a black field with the shahada in white. The Islamic Republic's flag was adopted on 19 August 2013, the 94th anniversary of Afghan independence from Britain.
flagColors: BlackRedGreenWhite
colorMeaningSummary: Black represents the dark history of Afghanistan and the many foreign invasions the country has endured, red represents the blood shed for Afghan independence, and green represents hope, prosperity and Islam. The white emblem in the center contains a mosque with a mihrab, a minbar, wheat sheaves and the shahada.
colorMeaningDetailed:
Black band

Represents the dark history of Afghanistan and the many foreign invasions that the country has resisted — from the Persian, Greek, Arab, Mongol and British empires. Black has been used on Afghan flags since the 18th century.

Red band

Represents the blood shed by Afghan patriots in the struggle for independence from Britain, achieved in 1919, and the sacrifices of the Afghan people throughout their history.

Green band

Represents hope, prosperity and Islam — the dominant religion of Afghanistan. Green is the traditional color of Islam and appears on many Muslim national flags.

Central emblem

The white emblem in the center contains a mosque with a mihrab (prayer niche) and a minbar (pulpit), flanked by wheat sheaves, with the shahada above and the year 1298 in the Islamic calendar below. The wheat sheaves represent agriculture and prosperity, and the shahada represents the Islamic faith of the Afghan people.

Contested status

Since the Taliban takeover in August 2021, the Islamic Republic's flag has been used by Afghan embassies and representatives abroad, while the Taliban government uses a black flag with the shahada. The United Nations and most foreign governments have not recognized the Taliban government or its flag, and continue to recognize the Islamic Republic's flag as the national flag of Afghanistan.
flagHistory: Afghanistan has changed its flag more often than almost any other country, reflecting its turbulent political history. Since 1880, the country has used at least 20 different national flags. The black-red-green tricolor was first adopted in 1928 under King Amanullah Khan, briefly removed, and restored in 1930. Since then, the flag has been changed many times — during the monarchy, the republic (1973), the communist era (1978 and 1980), the mujahideen government (1992), the Taliban's first rule (1996–2001), and the Islamic Republic (2001). The version adopted on 19 August 2013 removed the date 1348 from the emblem and standardized the design. After the Taliban retook power in 2021, the Islamic Republic's flag continued to be used by the country's representatives abroad and by resistance movements within Afghanistan.
flagDesigner: Based on the 1928 tricolor design, with the current emblem
similarFlagsAnswer: No other national flag closely resembles Afghanistan's. The combination of black, red and green vertical bands with a white emblem is unique.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

Afghanistan has used more than 20 different national flags across its history.

  • Emirate of Afghanistan (1880–1901): Plain black flag.
  • Emirate of Afghanistan (1901–1919): Black flag with a white emblem.
  • Kingdom of Afghanistan (1919–1928): Black field with the royal emblem.
  • First tricolor (1928–1929): Black, red and green tricolor with the royal emblem.
  • Kingdom of Afghanistan (1930–1973): Black, red and green with the national emblem.
  • Republic of Afghanistan (1973–1978): Same design with a modified emblem.
  • Communist era (1978–1992): Various designs including a Soviet-style flag.
  • Islamic State (1992–1996): Black, red and green with the shahada and sword.
  • Taliban (1996–2001): Plain white flag with the shahada.
  • Islamic Republic (2001–2021): Black, red and green with the national emblem.
  • Taliban (2021–present): Black field with the shahada (contested, not internationally recognized).

title: Cyprus
flagPageTitle: Flag of Cyprus — Colors, Meaning & History
flagMetaDescription: Flag of Cyprus: a copper island map above crossed olive branches on a white field. Learn its colors, meaning, adoption date (1960) and history.
flagMetaKeywords: cyprus flag, flag of cyprus, cypriot flag, cyprus flag colors, cyprus flag meaning, olive branches flag
flagSubtitle: A copper island map above crossed olive branches on a white field — the flag of the Republic of Cyprus.
flagQuickAnswer: The flag of Cyprus is a white field with a copper-orange outline of the island of Cyprus in the center, above two crossed green olive branches. The proportion is 3:5.
flagDescription: The Cypriot flag consists of a white field with a copper-orange silhouette of the island of Cyprus in the center, above two crossed green olive branches. The proportion is 3:5. It was adopted on 16 August 1960, when Cyprus gained independence from Britain, following a design competition that sought a symbol free of Greek or Turkish associations.
flagColors: WhiteCopperGreen
colorMeaningSummary: White represents peace and the desire for peaceful coexistence between the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities, copper represents the island's copper ore deposits — for which Cyprus has been famous since antiquity — and the green olive branches represent peace and the two communities of the island.
colorMeaningDetailed:
White field

Represents peace and the desire for peaceful coexistence between the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities. The use of white was deliberate — it was chosen to avoid the blue and red of the Greek flag and the red and white of the Turkish flag, both of which were associated with one community or the other.

Copper island silhouette

The copper-orange silhouette of Cyprus represents the island's copper ore deposits, which have been mined since the Bronze Age. The name 'Cyprus' is derived from the Greek word for copper (kypros), and the island was a major source of copper for the ancient Mediterranean world. The specific shade of copper used on the flag is a deliberate reference to this heritage.

Olive branches

The two crossed green olive branches beneath the island represent peace and the two main communities of Cyprus — the Greek Cypriots and the Turkish Cypriots. The olive branch has been a symbol of peace since antiquity and is mentioned in both Greek and Turkish traditions.

Design intention

The flag was designed to be neutral — it deliberately avoids both the blue and white of the Greek flag and the red and white of the Turkish flag. The design was chosen through a competition in 1960, and the winning design was by İsmet Güney, a Turkish Cypriot artist.
flagHistory: Cyprus was a British colony from 1878 until 1960, when it gained independence on 16 August 1960 after a four-year armed struggle by the Greek Cypriot EOKA movement. The new republic needed a flag that would represent both the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities, so a design competition was held. The winning design, by Turkish Cypriot artist İsmet Güney, featured a copper-orange silhouette of the island above two crossed olive branches on a white field. The flag was adopted on 16 August 1960, the day of independence, and has remained the flag of the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus since — though it is not used in the Turkish-occupied northern part of the island, which uses the flag of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (recognized only by Turkey).
flagDesigner: İsmet Güney
similarFlagsAnswer: No other national flag closely resembles Cyprus's. The combination of a white field with a copper island silhouette and crossed olive branches is unique.
flagVariants:
Historical and related flags

Cyprus has used several flags across its Ottoman, British and independence periods.

  • Ottoman Cyprus (1571–1878): Ottoman flag used during Ottoman rule.
  • British Cyprus (1878–1960): British Blue Ensign with a colonial badge featuring two lions.
  • Current flag (1960–present): White field with copper island and olive branches.
  • Presidential standard: Uses the Cypriot coat of arms with a dove and olive branch.
  • Northern Cyprus flag (1984–present): White field with red crescent and star and two red stripes, used by the unrecognized Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus.

flagDescription: The Maltese flag consists of two equal vertical bands of white (hoist) and red (fly). In the upper hoist corner of the white band is the George Cross — a silver cross with the inscription 'For Gallantry' on a blue background. The proportion is 2:3. The flag was adopted on 21 September 1964, when Malta gained independence from Britain, and was retained when Malta became a republic in 1974.
flagColors: WhiteRedBlue
colorMeaningSummary: White represents peace, purity and the light of the Mediterranean, and red represents the blood shed for Maltese independence and the courage of the Maltese people. According to tradition, the colors date back to the time of Roger I of Sicily, who gave them to the Maltese in 1091. The George Cross represents Malta's bravery during World War II.
colorMeaningDetailed:
White band

Represents peace, purity and the light of the Mediterranean. White was traditionally associated with the Maltese people's peaceful character and their historic Christian faith.

Red band

Represents the blood shed by Maltese patriots in defense of their island and the courage of the Maltese people. Red is also a traditional color of Mediterranean and Mediterranean island flags.

George Cross

Represents Malta's bravery during World War II, when the island was heavily bombed by Italian and German forces from 1940 to 1942. King George VI awarded the George Cross — the highest civilian award for gallantry in the United Kingdom — to the island of Malta on 15 April 1942, in recognition of the population's endurance. The medal appears on the flag as a silver cross with a blue border, inscribed with the words 'For Gallantry'.
flagHistory: Malta was a British colony from 1814 until 1964, when it gained independence on 21 September 1964. The white-and-red flag has been associated with the Maltese islands since at least the 13th century, when tradition says it was given to the Maltese by Roger I of Sicily in 1091. During the British colonial period, the flag was used with the Maltese coat of arms in the canton of a blue ensign. When Malta gained independence in 1964, the plain white-and-red design was adopted as the national flag, with the George Cross added to the upper hoist corner. The George Cross had been awarded to Malta in 1942, and its inclusion on the flag reflects the country's wartime experience. The flag was retained when Malta became a republic in 1974. It has remained unchanged since.
flagDesigner: Based on the traditional Maltese white-and-red flag, with the George Cross added in 1943
similarFlagsAnswer: No other national flag closely resembles Malta's. The combination of white and red vertical bands with the George Cross in the canton is unique.
flagVariants:

  • Current flag (1964–present): White and red vertical bands with the George Cross.
  • Presidential standard: Uses the Maltese coat of arms on a blue field.

colorMeaningDetailed:
Yellow band

The traditional papal color of gold, representing the Pope's spiritual authority, wisdom and the divine light. Yellow and gold have been associated with the Papacy since the Middle Ages and appeared on the banners of the Papal States.

White band

Represents purity, peace and the Pope's role as the spiritual leader of the Catholic Church. White is also the traditional color of the Pope's robes.

Papal coat of arms

Features two crossed keys beneath a papal tiara. The keys — one gold and one silver — represent the keys of Saint Peter, which Christ gave him in the Gospel of Matthew with the words 'I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven'. The gold key represents spiritual authority and the silver key represents temporal authority. The papal tiara (triregnum) — a three-tiered crown — represents the Pope's threefold authority as teacher, priest and ruler.

Square shape

Like Switzerland's flag, the Vatican City flag is square — the only two square national flags in the world. The Swiss Guard, the Pope's ceremonial bodyguard, uses a square flag based on the Vatican design.
flagHistory: The Papal States, which existed from 754 to 1870, used a variety of flags over the centuries, including yellow and red designs and white and gold designs. When Italian forces captured Rome in 1870, the Papal States were dissolved and the Pope became a 'prisoner in the Vatican'. In 1929, the Lateran Treaty between the Holy See and Italy established Vatican City as an independent sovereign state, and the current flag was adopted on 7 June 1929. The design combined the traditional papal colors of yellow and white with the papal coat of arms, and the square shape was chosen to distinguish it from other national flags. The flag has remained unchanged since, making it one of the most recognizable religious and national flags in the world.
flagDesigner: Based on the historic papal colors and coat of arms
similarFlagsAnswer: Switzerland and Vatican City are the only two countries in the world with square national flags. Switzerland uses a white cross on a red field, while Vatican City uses yellow and white vertical bands with the papal coat of arms.

colorMeaningDetailed:
Red field

Represents the blood shed by Albanian patriots during the centuries-long struggle for independence, from the medieval resistance against the Ottoman Empire to the declaration of independence in 1912. Red is also a traditional color of bravery and strength in Albanian culture.

Double-headed eagle

The black double-headed eagle is the national symbol of Albania and represents the Albanian nation. It has been used as a symbol by Albanian rulers since the Middle Ages, most famously by Gjergj Kastrioti Skanderbeg — the 15th-century Albanian national hero — who led the resistance against the Ottoman Empire for 25 years and used a red flag with a black double-headed eagle. The double-headed eagle represents the union of the Albanian people and their unity across borders — Albania, Kosovo, North Macedonia, Montenegro and the Albanian diaspora.

Design history

According to tradition, the eagle's wings form the shape of the letter 'Sh' when viewed in combination — a reference to Shqipëria, the Albanian name for Albania. The flag used during the communist era (1946–1992) added a gold-bordered red star above the eagle, which was removed in 1992 when the communist government fell.
flagHistory: Albania was part of the Ottoman Empire from the 15th century until 1912, when it declared independence on 28 November 1912. The flag was raised on the day of the declaration in Vlorë, based on the banner used by Skanderbeg in the 15th century. The design has been modified several times — during the Kingdom of Albania (1928–1939), a crown was added; during the Italian occupation (1939–1943), the flag was used with Italian elements; and during the communist period (1946–1992), a gold-bordered red star was added above the eagle. After the fall of communism, the plain red flag with the black double-headed eagle was restored on 7 April 1992. It has remained unchanged since.
flagDesigner: Based on the banner of Skanderbeg (15th century)
similarFlagsAnswer: No other national flag closely resembles Albania's. The combination of a red field with a black double-headed eagle is unique, though the double-headed eagle is also used as a symbol by Serbia, Montenegro, Russia and other countries with Byzantine or Balkan heritage.

Golden sun

The eight rays of the sun extend from the central disc to the edges of the flag, symbolizing the spread of freedom and light in all directions.

Design origin

The current design was adopted in 1995 after a dispute with Greece over the use of the Vergina Sun — a symbol of the ancient kingdom of Macedon that Greece also claimed as part of its cultural heritage. flagHistory: North Macedonia declared independence from Yugoslavia on 8 September 1991, following a referendum. The first flag, adopted on 11 August 1992, featured the Vergina Sun — a stylized sixteen-rayed sun symbol that had been discovered in the tomb of Philip II of Macedon at Vergina in Greece. Greece objected strongly to the use of this symbol, considering it part of Greek cultural heritage, and imposed a trade embargo on Macedonia from 1994 to 1995. As part of the Interim Accord signed on 13 September 1995, Macedonia agreed to change its flag, and the current design was adopted on 5 October 1995. The flag has remained unchanged since, including after the country changed its name to North Macedonia in 2019 as part of the Prespa Agreement with Greece.

Golden double-headed eagle

The double-headed eagle is a traditional symbol of the Montenegrin ruling dynasties, the Petrović-Njegoš and later the Karađorđević families. flagHistory: Montenegro has a long history as an independent principality and kingdom before joining the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (later Yugoslavia) in 1918. After Yugoslavia dissolved in the 1990s, Montenegro remained in a union with Serbia, and in 2004 the Montenegrin parliament adopted the current flag — restoring the historic red field with golden border and the double-headed eagle. colorMeaningDetailed:
Blue field

Represents Europe and the European Union, and is drawn from the flag of the European Union. Blue also represents peace and stability — a central hope for post-war Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Yellow triangle

Represents the three constituent peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina — Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs — and the approximate shape of the country. The triangle also symbolizes the country's balance between its three main ethnic groups.

White stars

Represent the country's aspiration to join the European Union — an aspiration shared by all three constituent peoples. The seven stars along the hypotenuse are white, and the top and bottom stars are cut in half by the flag's edges, symbolizing the country's ongoing path toward European integration. The seven stars also represent the seven countries that border Bosnia and Herzegovina — Croatia, Serbia and Montenegro (land borders) and Italy, Slovenia, Hungary and Romania (via the Adriatic Sea, which Bosnia and Herzegovina touches at Neum).

Design origin

The flag was designed by Carlos Westendorp, the High Representative of the international community in Bosnia and Herzegovina, after the Bosnian parliament failed to agree on a design. It was adopted on 4 February 1998 and deliberately avoids any reference to the country's three main ethnic groups or historic symbols, to prevent one group from feeling excluded.
flagHistory: Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence from Yugoslavia on 1 March 1992, following a referendum boycotted by most Bosnian Serbs. The first flag was a white field with a blue shield bearing the golden fleur-de-lis of the medieval Bosnian kingdom. This flag was used by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the Bosnian War (1992–1995), but was not accepted by the country's Serb and Croat communities. After the Dayton Agreement ended the war in 1995, the new state needed a flag that would be acceptable to all three communities. The Bosnian parliament failed to agree on a design, so the High Representative, Carlos Westendorp, imposed the current flag on 4 February 1998. It has remained unchanged since.
flagDesigner: Carlos Westendorp, High Representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina
similarFlagsAnswer: No other national flag closely resembles Bosnia and Herzegovina's. The combination of a blue field with a yellow triangle and a diagonal line of white stars is unique, though the blue field with white stars is drawn from the European Union flag.

colorMeaningDetailed:
Blue field

Represents the sky over Kosovo and the country's aspiration to join the European Union and NATO. Blue is also the dominant color of the European Union flag, emphasizing Kosovo's European orientation.

Golden map

The golden-yellow silhouette of the country represents the territory of Kosovo and its unity as a sovereign state. Gold is also a traditional color of wealth and prosperity, and Kosovo has significant mineral resources including lignite, lead, zinc and gold.

Six white stars

Represent the six ethnic communities of Kosovo — the Albanian majority, Serbs, Turks, Gorani, Roma and Bosniaks. The stars are arranged in an arc above the country's silhouette, emphasizing the unity of all communities within the state. In the original design, the six stars represented the six ethnic communities officially recognized by the Kosovar constitution.

Design origin

The flag was designed by Muhamer Ibrahimi and was chosen from a competition that received nearly 1,000 entries. It was adopted on 17 February 2008, the day Kosovo declared independence. The design deliberately avoids the red and black of the Albanian flag and the red, blue and white of the Serbian flag, to appear neutral and inclusive of all ethnic communities.
flagHistory: Kosovo was an autonomous province within Serbia from 1945 until 1989, when Serbia revoked its autonomy. Throughout the 1990s, Kosovar Albanians sought greater autonomy and eventually independence, leading to the Kosovo War (1998–1999) and NATO intervention. After the war, Kosovo was administered by the United Nations under UN Security Council Resolution 1244. On 17 February 2008, Kosovo declared independence from Serbia and adopted the current flag. The flag was designed by Muhamer Ibrahimi and chosen from a national competition. It has been recognized by over 100 UN member states, though Serbia continues to claim Kosovo as its territory, and the flag is not universally recognized.

colorMeaningDetailed:
Yellow field

Represents the Sultan of Brunei and the royal family. Yellow is the traditional color of Malay royalty and has been used by the Brunei sultanate since the 14th century. The specific shade of yellow used is a bright golden-yellow, reflecting the country's royal heritage.

White and black diagonal stripes

Represent the two chief ministers — the Pengiran Bendahara (Prime Minister) and the Pengiran Pemancha (Minister of Home Affairs) — who served as joint regents of Brunei during the minority of Sultan Ahmad Tajuddin in the 1920s and 1930s. The white stripe represents the Pengiran Bendahara and the black stripe the Pengiran Pemancha.

Red national crest

The red national crest is the central emblem of the flag and represents the Sultan's authority. It consists of a crescent (the symbol of Islam), a hand (representing the power of the Sultan to protect his people), a pair of wings (representing the four cardinal virtues — justice, peace, prosperity and tranquility), and a central mast with the flag of Brunei. Below the crescent is a ribbon with the national motto 'Always in service with God's guidance'.

The design combined the traditional yellow of the Brunei royal family with the black-and-white stripes of the two regents and the red national crest. The flag was retained when Brunei became fully independent on 1 January 1984 and has remained unchanged since.

The number twelve is deliberately fixed and does not change with the number of EU member states — it was chosen because twelve is a traditional symbol of completeness and perfection (twelve months in a year, twelve hours on a clock, twelve signs of the zodiac, twelve apostles).

Circle of stars

The stars form a circle, representing the unity of the European peoples. The circle also evokes a crown or a halo, in a symbolic reference to the Virgin Mary — an association that was deliberately downplayed when the flag was adopted by the European Communities, to make the design more inclusive of non-Christian Europeans.

The design was created by Arsène Heitz, a French designer who worked for the Council of Europe, and was adopted by the Council of Europe on 8 December 1955. The design was chosen from over 100 proposals, and the twelve-star circle was selected after some debate about whether the number should correspond to the number of member states (which was then more than twelve). The Council of Europe decided on the fixed number twelve to avoid any implication of exclusion. In 1986, the European Communities (later the European Union) adopted the same flag as its own, and it has been used by both organizations since.

It was adopted by the Council of Europe on 8 December 1955, and first raised in Strasbourg on 13 December 1955. For three decades, the flag was used only by the Council of Europe. In 1986, the European Communities (the precursor to the European Union) adopted the same design as its own flag, and it was raised for the first time at the Berlaymont building in Brussels on 29 May 1986. The flag has been used by the European Union since its formal establishment in 1993 and has remained unchanged since.
flagDesigner: Arsène Heitz and Paul M. G. Lévy

It is also the basis for the flags of several other regions and territories that were historically part of the Crown of Aragon, including Aragon, Valencia, the Balearic Islands, Roussillon, Andorra and the city of Barcelona. The Senyera is used as the official flag of the autonomous community of Catalonia within Spain.
