Four red stripes

Represent the four red bars (pals) on the coat of arms of the House of Barcelona. According to the 14th-century legend, Wilfred the Hairy, Count of Barcelona, was mortally wounded in battle against the Normans and dipped his fingers in his own blood, drawing four stripes across his golden shield — creating the emblem of his dynasty. The historical origin of the stripes is uncertain, but they appear on the seal of Ramon Berenguer IV, Count of Barcelona, in the 12th century.

Heraldic origin

The design is one of the oldest coats of arms in Europe, dating to at least the 12th century. It was the emblem of the counts of Barcelona, and when the House of Barcelona inherited the Kingdom of Aragon in 1137, the stripes became the emblem of the Crown of Aragon — a confederation that at its height included Catalonia, Aragon, Valencia, the Balearic Islands, Sicily, Sardinia, Naples and Athens.

Senyera vs Estelada

The Senyera is the official flag of Catalonia. A related flag, the Estelada, adds a blue triangle with a white star (or a yellow triangle with a red star for socialist variants) to the Senyera and is used by supporters of Catalan independence. The Estelada is not an official flag and is not used by the Catalan government.
flagHistory: The Senyera has been in use since at least the 12th century, when the four red stripes on a golden field appeared on the seals of the counts of Barcelona. As the counts of Barcelona became kings of Aragon, the design spread across the Crown of Aragon and its territories, and it became the emblem of Catalonia, Aragon, Valencia and the Balearic Islands. In the modern era, the Senyera was adopted as the official flag of the autonomous community of Catalonia when the region's statute of autonomy was approved in 1979, following the end of Franco's dictatorship (during which Catalan symbols were suppressed). The flag was retained in the 2006 statute of autonomy and remains the official flag of Catalonia today. The Estelada, a variant used by the independence movement, has been widely used since the early 20th century but is not an official symbol.

The oak is the most important symbol of Basque liberty and self-government, and its image appears on the Basque coat of arms. The green saltire also represents the green mountains that dominate the Basque landscape.

Design origin

The Ikurriña was designed in 1894 by Sabino Arana and his brother Luis Arana — the founders of the Basque Nationalist Party (PNV) — originally as a flag for the province of Biscay. It was later adopted as the flag of the entire Basque Country. Arana designed the flag based on the historic coats of arms of the Basque provinces, combining the red field of Biscay, the white cross of the old flag of Bilbao and the green saltire of the Oak of Gernika.
flagHistory: The Basque Country is a historic region spanning parts of northern Spain and southwestern France. During the Second Spanish Republic (1931–1939), the flag was used unofficially by Basque autonomous institutions, and it was formally adopted as the flag of the Basque Autonomous Community after the Spanish transition to democracy. The Basque Statute of Autonomy, approved in 1979, recognized the Ikurriña as the official flag of the Basque Country. The flag has remained the most recognizable symbol of Basque identity and is used across the Basque Country in Spain — though it is not officially recognized in the French Basque Country (Iparralde).

Red cross

According to tradition, Saint George was a Roman soldier of Greek origin who was martyred for his Christian faith around 303 CE. The cross itself is a simple heraldic cross (a cross throughout, meaning it extends to all four edges of the field).

Origin

The red cross on a white field was used by crusaders in the 12th and 13th centuries, and it became associated with England during the reign of King Edward I (1272–1307). By the 14th century, it was widely recognized as the flag of England, and it was used by English soldiers during the Hundred Years' War (1337–1453). The flag was formally adopted as the national flag of England in the 16th century and has remained in continuous use since.
flagHistory: The St George's Cross has been used as a symbol of England since the 13th century. The cross was originally associated with the Crusades, but it became specifically linked to England during the reign of King Edward I, who adopted Saint George as the patron saint of England. By the 14th century, the red cross on a white field was widely recognized as the flag of England and was used by English soldiers during the Hundred Years' War. In 1606, after the Union of the Crowns, the St George's Cross was combined with the Scottish saltire of St Andrew to create the first Union Flag. The St George's Cross remained the flag of England and was also used as part of the Union Jack. In the modern era, the flag has continued to be the official flag of England and is widely flown in England. Since 2000, it has been flown over government buildings in England on St George's Day (23 April), and it is used by English sports teams and at national events.

Represents the six counties of Northern Ireland — Antrim, Armagh, Down, Fermanagh, Londonderry (Derry) and Tyrone. The star has six points, unlike the five-pointed stars used in most heraldry, to reflect the six counties.

Red Hand of Ulster

The red right hand is the ancient symbol of the province of Ulster and the O'Neill dynasty. According to legend, the symbol originated when two chieftains raced to be the first to touch the shore of Ulster, and one cut off his hand and threw it ashore to win the race. The Red Hand has been used as a symbol of Ulster since the 13th century.

Crown

Represents the British monarchy and Northern Ireland's constitutional status as part of the United Kingdom. The crown is a traditional symbol of British royal authority.

Contested status

The Ulster Banner is used primarily by unionist and loyalist communities and is not recognized by many nationalists and republicans, who favor the Irish tricolor or a neutral flag. flagHistory: Northern Ireland was created in 1921 when the island of Ireland was partitioned, with the six northeastern counties remaining part of the United Kingdom. In 1953, the Ulster Banner was officially adopted as the flag of Northern Ireland. In 1972, the Northern Ireland Parliament was suspended, and in 1973 it was abolished, leaving Northern Ireland without a legislature and without an official flag. Several attempts have been made to establish a new, neutral flag that would be acceptable to both unionists and nationalists, but none have succeeded. Today, the Ulster Banner remains the most widely recognized flag associated with Northern Ireland, but it is used primarily by the unionist community and is not recognized as a neutral symbol for the whole region.

colorMeaningDetailed:
Blue field

Represents the sky over Scotland and the seas that surround the country's long coastline. The exact shade of blue has varied over the centuries — the current official shade is Pantone 300, a bright medium blue.

White saltire

Represents Saint Andrew, the patron saint of Scotland. According to Christian tradition, Saint Andrew was crucified on an X-shaped cross (a saltire) because he felt unworthy to be crucified on the same type of cross as Jesus. He is said to have preached in Scythia and possibly in Scotland, and his relics were brought to St Andrews in Fife. Saint Andrew became the patron saint of Scotland in the 9th century.

Legend of Athelstaneford

According to tradition, the flag originated on the eve of the Battle of Athelstaneford in 832 CE. King Óengus II of the Picts was preparing to fight a larger army of Angles when he saw a cloud formation in the blue sky that formed an X — the cross of Saint Andrew. He vowed that if he won the battle, he would make Saint Andrew the patron saint of Scotland. The next day, the Picts won, and Saint Andrew became the patron saint of Scotland.

Oldest flag

The Saltire is often described as the oldest national flag in continuous use, along with the Danish Dannebrog. The earliest documented use of the saltire as a Scottish emblem is from 1286, and the earliest image of a blue field with a white saltire is from 1512.
flagHistory: The Saltire has been used as a symbol of Scotland since at least the 13th century, when it appeared on the seals of Scottish nobles and on Scottish coins. According to tradition, the flag originated in 832 at the Battle of Athelstaneford. It was formally adopted as the national flag of Scotland in the 16th century and has been in continuous use since. In 1606, after the Union of the Crowns, the Saltire was combined with the English St George's Cross to create the first Union Flag. When Ireland joined the union in 1801, the cross of St Patrick was added to create the modern Union Jack. Despite this, the Saltire remained the national flag of Scotland and has continued to be flown throughout the country. In 2003, the Scottish Parliament standardized the proportions of the flag at 3:5, and in 2006, it was decided that the Saltire should be flown over Edinburgh Castle every day rather than just on St Andrew's Day (30 November).

Red dragon

The Y Ddraig Goch is the oldest and most important national symbol of Wales. It represents the Welsh people, their history and their resilience against conquest. The dragon has been associated with Wales since at least the 5th century and appears in the Mabinogion, the collection of medieval Welsh tales, where the red dragon fights the white dragon (representing the Saxons). The red dragon was used as a symbol by Welsh kings and princes, including Cadwaladr and Owain Glyndŵr, and was brought to prominence by Henry Tudor, who used it as one of his supporters on the royal arms when he became King Henry VII in 1485.

The red dragon was used by Owain Glyndŵr during his rebellion against English rule in the early 15th century and by Henry Tudor at the Battle of Bosworth in 1485. The design was used as part of the royal arms of England from 1485 until 1603, but the purely Welsh flag fell out of use after the Acts of Union. In 1953, the flag was used at the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II, and in 1959 it was officially adopted as the national flag of Wales in its current form — a red dragon on a white and green field. In 2005, the Welsh flag was granted official status in the United Kingdom, and it is now flown over government buildings in Wales on St David's Day (1 March) and other occasions.

The flag of Saint Helena shows a shield with a ship, cliffs and a wirebird; the flag of Ascension Island shows a shield with a ship, turtles and seabirds; and the flag of Tristan da Cunha shows a shield with a longboat, a Tristan rock lobster and a volcano.
